q8.answer: Session records live in one new Redis instance on the private network, stored under the key `sess:` plus the SHA-256 hash of the sid, with fields uid, created_at and abs_exp. Either app instance receives a request, hashes the cookie's sid, and reads the same Redis key, so no sticky sessions are needed.

q9.answer: Failure timestamps live in a Redis sorted set keyed `fail:` plus the SHA-256 hash of the lowercased email. On each failed attempt, one Lua script adds the new timestamp, removes entries older than 10 minutes measured back from that attempt, and counts what remains; a count of 5 or more sets the 15-minute lock and deletes the set.

q10.answer: The server checks that the session key still exists in Redis, which means the idle TTL has not run out, and that the current time is before the abs_exp stored in the record. If both hold, it resets the key's TTL to min(30 minutes, abs_exp minus now); if abs_exp has passed, it deletes the key and treats the request as signed out.

q11.answer: The browser receives HTTP 503 with the message "Sign-in is temporarily unavailable. Try again in a minute." and no Set-Cookie, so no session is created and the failed-attempt count is not recorded. The design does not spell out whether an old session already deleted before the failed write is restored, so that edge is not decided.

q12.answer: No sweeper job exists; Redis TTLs remove everything. The session key expires after at most 30 minutes of inactivity (or at abs_exp, whichever is sooner), the failure set expires 10 minutes after its last entry, and the lock expires after 15 minutes.
